rv.q: McPherson and Dunster's adaptation is ambitious and spectacular
Sadly for the producers, the practicalities of live performance can't touch the roller-coaster ride of the film.
The whole extravaganza, involving heart-in-mouth aerial work, gouts of flame and nifty visual effects, feels more like a circus-style parade of tricks than an involving theatrical narrative.
The auditorium feels like a gameshow space with immersive moving seats
This team has staged The Hunger Games with all the bells, bangs and whistles you’d expect, but it hasn’t truly understood the appeal of its source material

It never lectures you on its themes, it’s just obvious what they are, and it’s at least as good on Katniss’s bemused dabbling with the world of celebrity as the fighty stuff – Nathan Ives-Moiba gives a very nice turn as Cinna, Katniss’s flamboyant but nurturing stylist.
But this is an arena of spectacle, not soul; of sensation but not emotion.
Conor McPherson (who wrote The Weir) fails to give a third dimension to Katniss’s character, so newcomer Mia Carragher can’t make us care about her. The set pieces aren’t much cop either.
Yet despite all this, though visually impressive and sometimes ingenious, the resulting show proves a curiously empty spectacle.
I’m disappointed to report that I found this unexcitingly staged spectacle an underwhelming trudge.

Intriguingly, McPherson admits in a programme note that he initially conceived of his script as a conversation taking place around a kitchen table with minimal props, leaving it to the audience’s imagination to fill in the gaps. How one wishes that...
It’s not the fault of the actors that the effect is humdrum.
The Hunger Games on Stage is a show that should be on everybody’s Christmas list.
For this does feel more like a show than a play; for the most part character is lost amid the sheer scale of the visual enterprise.
And we crave more than this production ultimately delivers.

Too long has been spent on looks and not enough importance has been given to the exploration of the themes. The sociopolitical allegories and the symbolism are mere afterthoughts of a grand spectacle. We don’t truly witness the wealth gap between the Districts, nor do we absorb the reason why the Games exist.
There are a few theatrical flourishes here and there, but fundamentally, this felt like high-end theme park entertainment with nothing new added to the source material to commend it.

Even rich questions don’t stop the lingering frustration that the show doesn’t quite decide what it wants to be, caught between introspection and bombast and never allowing the two to support one-another.
This production could have been spectacular, and in fact I was wiling it to be so, but it is unfortunately style over substance with little atmosphere, missed opportunities and frustrating staging.
Despite the athletic cast’s tireless efforts, this is a strangely unsatisfying experience.
The most magnetic performance of the night belongs to someone who never steps on stage
Small children may enjoy this show but anyone over 13 will be bored senseless.
Either this emotional alienation is a disguised Brechtian technique, or the adaptation is a brilliant pyrotechnic gymnastics show, where the political themes inevitably come second.
Ticketholders will get their money's worth in spectacle, while perhaps missing the emotional connection of the books and movie.
The show is visually entertaining, but it lacks the heart to make you care about the fate of Panem’s people.

cn.t: Critics find this ambitious spectacle visually dazzling but emotionally hollow, with impressive production design and effects failing to compensate for a lack of innovative storytelling beyond the familiar film adaptation.
